title: Author pages that are real
metaTitle: Author pages that name a real studio
excerpt: An author page should say who the studio is and link the pieces they stand behind. A byline of Admin helps neither a buyer nor a citation.

faqs.question: What should a studio author page include?
faqs.answer: Say who the studio is, what it designs and builds, and which published pieces it stands behind. Link those pieces. A short note on how the work is done is enough. A fake biography, a stock portrait, and a list of awards you did not earn are worse than a plain page.

faqs.question: Is a studio byline acceptable, or does it have to be a person?
faqs.answer: A studio byline is acceptable when the studio really wrote and reviewed the piece, and the author page explains that practice. A named person is better when that person will remain accountable for the words. What does not work is a shared login called Admin, Staff, or Editor with no page behind it.

faqs.question: Do bylines help search and citations?
faqs.answer: They help a person, and a system, see who created the page. Google's people-first guidance treats a byline that leads to real background as part of making authorship clear. A byline that leads nowhere, or to a page that could belong to any agency, does not do that work.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Blog author page SEO starts with a page that says who the studio is and links the pieces they stand behind. A byline of Admin does not help a buyer, and it does not help a citation. The reader cannot tell whose judgment they are being asked to trust.

If the writing is part of how you sell the practice, the byline is part of the product. Treat it with the same care as the homepage.

## Admin is not an author

Admin is a database default. It shows up when the CMS required a user and nobody wanted to decide. Staff, Editor, and Team are the same shrug in a nicer font. A founder reading an essay about their own kind of problem will look for a name, or at least a studio, and then look for proof that the name has done the work. A dead-end byline says the words were attached to an account, not to a practice.

This is not a request to invent personalities. A fake author with a generated portrait is worse than Admin, because it adds a lie. If the studio writes as a studio, say that. If one person drafts and another reviews, say that in a sentence. The standard is accuracy. [Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) puts the question directly: is it obvious who created the content, do pages carry a byline where a reader would expect one, and does that byline lead to further information about the author and the areas they write about? Those are the requirements. A portrait and a witty bio are optional. A true destination for the byline is not.

The same page warns against content that is mass-produced or spread so thin that individual pieces get no care. An author line of Admin is often the signature of that process. Even when the essay was careful, the byline tells the other story. Fix the byline so it matches the care.

Google's title guidance is relevant in a smaller way. It tells you not to title a specific person's profile "Profile," because that word does not say whose page it is. "Author" and "Team" have the same problem. The title of the page should name the studio or the person. A stranger arriving from search should know, before they scroll, whose work this is.

## What the page should say

Say what the studio does, in the words you use with a client. Hanabi designs and builds. The public work includes Down the Cove, an ecommerce migration and redesign; Thomas Bewick, an editorial heritage site; Ballarat Box Sports; Wabisabi; Got Next; Leadly; and Trade Moai. The stack on the sites is Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, and, where the product needs it, Motion, Prisma, and PostgreSQL, deployed on Vercel. Design work happens in Figma, Framer, and Illustrator. That is a real practice. An author page can say it without turning into a résumé full of numbers nobody asked you to prove.

Say how the writing is produced. Drafted from project work, reviewed before it is published, corrected when a tool or a recommendation changes. You do not need a manifesto. You need a reader to understand that the essays are part of the studio, not a side project fed by a prompt and a calendar.

Say what you will not pretend. Do not invent revenue, headcount, awards, timelines, or client quotes. Do not borrow a client's praise from a sales call and put it under a portrait. If a project is public, you may name it and describe the kind of work. If it is not public, leave it off. The author page is a public page. It lives by the same rule as the portfolio.

Link a way to talk. One path is enough. The page is not a second homepage, and it should not compete with the homepage for every service you offer. A short paragraph and a link to the work, or to a conversation, will do. Founders who wanted a biography and found a sales page will go back to the essay disappointed. Founders who wanted to know if you are real will stay if the page is specific.

## Link the pieces you stand behind

The most useful thing on the page is the list. Every published essay that carries this byline should be reachable from here, with its title and a one-line summary. Orphaned posts, the ones that exist in the index and nowhere else, feel accidental. Posts that are listed under an author and also linked from the relevant service page feel like a body of work.

Keep the list current. When you unpublish or redirect a piece, remove it. When you update a piece because the answer changed, the title on this page should match. A stale title on the author page is a small version of an obsolete heading. It tells a returning reader that nobody is watching.

Group the list only if the groups are real. Websites, product design, brand, engineering. Those are useful if they match how a buyer looks. A group called "Thought leadership" is not useful. It is a label for posts you could not categorize, which usually means the posts were written to fill a quota.

Do not list work the studio does not stand behind. A guest post you disagree with, a draft that leaked, a syndicated copy on another domain: leave them off, or explain the relationship in one clause. The page is an endorsement. Treat inclusion as a decision, not as an automatic query of every row in the CMS.

If several people write, each person gets a page, and the studio page links to them. Do not merge everyone into one bio to save a template. A founder trying to hire you wants to know whether the person who wrote the careful essay about checkout is the person who would be on the project. If the answer is "the studio reviews together," say that, and mean it. If the answer is a specific designer or engineer, the byline should already have said so.

## A studio name or a person's name

Both can be honest. A studio name fits when the work is reviewed as a group and you do not want a single face to become the only reason a client calls. A person's name fits when that person is the one a reader should hold responsible, and when they are willing to have the essay follow them. The failure is mixing the two without saying so: a person's portrait, a studio voice, and no indication of who approved the advice.

Hanabi can write as Hanabi. The author page then has to carry the practice: what the studio makes, which public projects show it, and how a piece gets from notes to a published URL. That is more credible than five thin bios for roles you do not have. It is also more credible than a single founder myth if the work is done by the studio. Choose the version that matches the engagement a client would actually buy.

If you later add a person, do not rewrite history on old posts in a way that implies they wrote pieces from before they arrived. Authorship is a fact. Update it when it was wrong. Leave it when it was right.

## What a buyer and a citation both need

A buyer uses the page as a trust check. They read an essay, click the byline, and ask: is this a studio that has done the thing, or a site that publishes about the thing? The list of pieces, the named projects, and the absence of fake proof answer faster than a slogan. [Selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is the other half of that check. The author page says who writes. The work says what has shipped. They should not contradict each other. If the essays are about ecommerce redesign and the work is about ecommerce redesign, a founder can connect them. If the essays are about everything and the work is about three careful projects, the author page is overselling the practice.

A citation needs the same facts for a different reason. Someone, or a system, quoting the piece should be able to say who said it. "Hanabi, a studio that designs and builds sites and products" is citable. "Admin" is not. Google's guidance treats clear authorship as part of how people judge experience and trust, especially where the topic can affect someone's money or safety. Most studio essays are not medical advice. Some of them are about billing, checkout, and the public face of a company. Those deserve a real byline even more. The habit should be the same on every piece, so you are not deciding authorship only when the topic feels serious.

Do not stuff the author page with the keyword you hope to rank for. The title can name the studio. The first paragraph can say you write about the work. A page that exists to rank for "author" and says nothing specific will lose to the essay the reader originally wanted. [Google's title guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) wants a descriptive title, not a vague label, and it will look at the visible heading when the title element is empty or generic. Give the page one obvious heading: the name.

## What not to build

Do not build a social network. Comments, follower counts, and badges add maintenance and almost no trust. Do not build a second blog index that competes with the real index. The author page lists this author's pieces. The blog index lists the writing. They can overlap. They should not be two designs.

Do not gate the page. It is public because the essays are public. Do not hide it in the footer only. The byline on each article is the front door. If the byline is not a link, the page does not exist for most readers, however beautiful it is.

Do not automate the bio from a job title and a city. "Designer in Austin writing about design" is the city-swapped page in miniature. Say the work. If you have nothing specific to say yet, publish fewer essays until you do. An empty author page full of intentions is a promise without pieces.

## After the byline, the body of work

Once the author is real, the next risk is the shape of the writing itself. A true byline on fifty interchangeable posts is still a mill. The posts have to be specific, they have to link to each other for a reason, and they have to point at an offer you actually sell.

That is the standard to hold before you add another piece. Look at the list on the author page and ask which decision each essay helps a founder make. If you cannot answer, the essay is not ready, or it does not belong under this name.

A cluster is how that list becomes a practice instead of a pile. [Topic clusters without a content mill](/blog/topic-clusters-without-a-content-mill) is the next piece, because a real author page should open onto a set of specific answers, not onto fifty variations of the same post.
